messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 60
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 68

He is a 60-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life in hospitality, moving through the ranks with the steady discipline of someone who knows how to keep a building running and a rooming house calm. As a hotel manager, he is used to solving problems before guests notice them, smoothing conflicts, checking details, and making sure everyone else is comfortable. He takes pride in that competence. He has been in a relationship for several years, and until the event that changed his life, he describes himself as organized, patient, and hard to rattle.

The trauma begins at work, in the place where he once felt most in control. One afternoon, while handling a maintenance issue in a service area, he is exposed to a toxic chemical. He remembers the sharp, unnatural smell first, then the sudden burning in his throat and chest. At the time, he does what he has always done in an emergency: he tries to stay calm, assess the situation, and protect other people. But his body reacts faster than his mind can organize. His breathing becomes difficult, his eyes water, and panic rises as he realizes something is very wrong. He leaves the area, but the sensation of contamination stays with him even after the immediate danger passes. He later describes the moment as the point when the world stopped feeling safe and predictable.

In the days after the exposure, he cannot let the event settle into the past. He replays the scene repeatedly, trying to figure out whether he missed a warning sign, whether he should have smelled it sooner, whether he made the wrong decision by staying as long as he did. He becomes preoccupied with the possibility that his lungs, throat, or heart were permanently damaged. Even when doctors tell him that the acute danger has passed, he remains unconvinced. He notices every change in his body—a cough, a tight chest, a dry throat—and immediately wonders if the chemical is still affecting him. He starts checking his pulse and monitoring his breathing, especially at night, when his body feels most vulnerable.

Sleep becomes difficult almost immediately. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes hours later with his chest tight and his mind racing. Sometimes he wakes with a start, feeling as though he is back in the service corridor, smelling the chemical again and struggling for air. On those nights, he gets out of bed and walks slowly through the house, opening windows, drinking water, sitting upright until the panic eases. His partner notices that he has become more alert and more withdrawn. He tries not to burden them, but he is easily irritated now, especially when someone suggests the exposure is behind him. He feels misunderstood, as if other people can choose to move on while he remains trapped in a body that keeps reminding him.

At work, the hotel no longer feels like the secure environment he once managed with ease. He starts avoiding the maintenance areas and delegating tasks he used to handle himself. He stays close to the front desk and the public spaces where he can see what is happening. He is more tense during inspections, more cautious around cleaning supplies, and more likely to ask staff what chemicals they are using. Strong odors can trigger a wave of nausea and dizziness that makes him want to leave the area immediately. He hates that he has become like this. He sees the change as weakness, even though he also recognizes how hard he is trying to keep functioning. He pushes himself to continue working because work gives him structure, but it now takes more effort to concentrate, and he sometimes loses track of conversations when his mind drifts back to the exposure.

Over time, his world becomes smaller. He avoids places that remind him of the incident, particularly enclosed utility rooms and industrial smells, and he is more hesitant in situations that involve uncertainty or poor ventilation. He no longer trusts his body in the way he once did. In quieter moments, he says he feels as though the chemical exposure took away not just his sense of safety, but his sense of mastery. He grieves the ease he used to have in moving through his workday without fear.

Even so, he keeps showing up. He still dresses carefully for work, greets staff professionally, and checks in on the hotel with the same sense of duty that has guided his life. But underneath that composed exterior, he remains on guard, scanning for danger, bracing for another mistake, another smell, another reminder that one ordinary workday was enough to leave him living differently from that point on.
